crime.value: Theft by 'rolling' a drunk: a B-girl drugs/liquors up ex-convict Beggs in a bar and steals the suitcase holding the $ he had hidden 20 years earlier (proceeds of the original robbery he served time for). Central question: who took the suitcase and where did it go?
crime.quote: "My suitcase," Beggs said distinctly, facing the man. "I want my suitcase, you understand?"

victim.value: Harry Beggs, 50-year-old newly released convict, white-haired, naive after 20 years inside, carrying untraceable stolen cash he cannot report — the perfect mark
victim.quote: It was there, still in the leather suitcase, all in cash, neatly bundled up by denomination

closed_world.value: The old neighborhood: Lucky's (formerly Mike's) bar and the tenement three flights up — only the bartender and the girl were present with the suitcase
closed_world.quote: "No girl works here, fella. You got the wrong idea about the kind of place I run."

culprit_and_motive.value: Angela, the pale girl in the cheap white pearls who works the bar — revealed to be Beggs' own daughter; motive: mercenary theft from an easy drunk mark
culprit_and_motive.quote: Angela tugged nervously at the strand of cheap dead-white pearls still around her throat.

resolution.value: Ironic recognition rather than justice: Beggs meets his never-seen daughter and identifies her by the dead-white pearls as the thief; no recovery, no arrest
resolution.quote: They looked at each other, the old man and the girl

investigator.value: The victim himself — Beggs, ex-convict protagonist whose limited, half-drunk viewpoint frames the whole story
investigator.quote: "The girl I was with. The one who worked here."

suspect_architecture.value: Narrow cast around a single theft: the B-girl who drugged and rolled Beggs (opportunity, motive: money), the ferret-faced bartender who denies everything (opportunity, plausible accomplice), and by implication the estranged wife Edith. The girl is revealed to be Beggs' own daughter Angela.
suspect_architecture.quote: "The girl I was with. The one who worked here." "No girl works here, fella."

red_herring.value: The bartender's hostility, contempt and blank denials steer suspicion onto him as thief or accomplice, deflecting from the girl and from her identity
red_herring.quote: "I didn't see your lousy suitcase. And no girl works here. If you got rolled by somebody, that's your business, not mine."

clue_fairness.value: Fairly planted physical clue: the cheap dead-white pearls and pale blonde prettiness of the bar girl are described in detail before the identical necklace appears on Angela in the closing line; also Beggs' own age-arithmetic about Edith and the drugged drink poured from a displayed bottle
clue_fairness.quote: the cheap dead-white pearls and the slim throat severed by a low black neckline

social_world.value: Post-prison underclass America: warden/ex-con power gap, decaying tenement neighborhood, a rough workingman's bar gentrified into a clip-joint cocktail lounge where a bartender tolerates a house B-girl; an abandoned wife who never visited and a daughter forced into the trade
social_world.quote: Lucky's was another sort of place altogether... jeweled up with chrome and colored glass, a lousy cocktail lounge.

alibi.value: The bartender's flat denial that any girl works there functions as a collective alibi for both; Angela's alibi is being asleep in her bedroom when her mother wakes her
alibi.quote: The blonde girl in the loose-fitting nightgown was yawning and blinking.

reveal_mechanic.value: Visual recognition rather than deduction: the same distinctive strand of cheap dead-white pearls worn by the bar girl is seen on Beggs' never-met daughter, silently confirming she robbed her own father
reveal_mechanic.quote: Angela tugged nervously at the strand of cheap dead-white pearls still around her throat.

media_and_audience.value: Institutional framing rather than press: the prison labels Beggs one of 'the innocent ones' who denies the theft, and the world reads him only as a harmless white-haired old man — a perception both protecting and victimizing him
media_and_audience.quote: "I remember now. You're one of the innocent ones."

investigator_wound.value: Beggs, his own investigator, is wounded by twenty lost years, old age and shame; his craving for kindness and human contact from a young woman is exactly what the crime exploits, and the truth destroys his reunion with his family
investigator_wound.quote: he hated to see even the false smile disappear.

victims_enemies.value: Beggs, the victim of the roll, has no enemies in the ordinary sense — the person who robs him is his own daughter Angela, who has never met him, and the wife Edith who never visited him in twenty years. The grievance web is familial abandonment: a wife who stopped coming, a child raised without a father, a neighborhood that has forgotten him. The bartender's contempt and denial ('no girl works here') completes the circle of indifference.
victims_enemies.quote: "Your wife wasn't much for visiting, was she?" "No."

suspect_wounds.value: Angela's vulnerability is her trade — a bar girl working a room whose owner denies she exists; she must deny and vanish or lose everything. The bartender's wound is his establishment's respectability ('You got the wrong idea about the kind of place I run'), which forces him to lie about the girl and so look complicit in the theft. Beggs' own wound is that he is a convicted thief protecting stolen money, so he can never report the robbery.
suspect_wounds.quote: "No girl works here, fella. You got the wrong idea about the kind of place I run."

unreliable_frame.value: The story is told close to Beggs, whose account cannot be trusted: he denies the theft to the Warden ('What money?') while going straight to the buried suitcase; he is drunk on his first whiskey in twenty years and drugged, so the crucial hour is a blackout narrated as a prison dream. The bartender's flat denial is a second false account, and Edith's warmth conceals what her daughter does at night.
unreliable_frame.quote: He was in the prison shop, the machines roaring... "Wake up, buddy."

setting_as_constraint.value: Twenty years of prison is the constraint: it makes Beggs an old man who cannot hold liquor, cannot recognize the changed neighborhood, and cannot know his own daughter's face. Mike's honest, brightly lit bar has become Lucky's — dark, chromed, 'too dark for an old pair of eyes' — an environment engineered for rolling drunks, which the girl exploits. And the stolen money's illegality means the police can never be called.
setting_as_constraint.quote: It was dark, too dark for an old pair of eyes, jeweled up with chrome and colored glass, a lousy cocktail lounge.

evidence_type.value: Physical/visual identification — a single object seen twice. The 'cheap dead-white pearls' worn by the bar girl reappear on Angela's throat in the last line, silently proving who took the suitcase. No forensic or documentary proof exists or ever could.
evidence_type.quote: Angela tugged nervously at the strand of cheap dead-white pearls still around her throat.

false_suspect.value: The ferret-faced bartender, who takes the full weight of Beggs' accusation — he served the doctored drinks, denied the girl's existence, and threw Beggs into the street — yet the theft was the girl's work, and his lie was to protect his own license, not the loot.

technical_detail.value: The B-girl con: a house girl befriends a lone drunk, gets him to buy rounds, takes hers 'with ginger ale' so she stays sober, moves him from the bar to a table out of the bartender's line of sight, and lets the liquor (on a stomach that hasn't had whiskey in two decades) do the rest. The numb foot and lost hours suggest the drink was more than whiskey.
technical_detail.quote: "Come to think of it, I'd like mine with ginger ale. Couldn't we sit at a table?"

moral_ambiguity.value: Angela is a girl raised fatherless in a decaying tenement by a worn-out mother, working a cocktail lounge to survive; she rolled an anonymous old drunk carrying a suitcase, not knowing he was her father returning with the family's money. The victim is himself a thief reclaiming stolen cash, and his own line — 'I'm one guy you can't blame for anything' — turns back on him: he blames no one, and the daughter cannot be blamed either. The punishment is exactly proportional and entirely undeserved by anyone.
moral_ambiguity.quote: kid, I'm one guy you never laid eyes on before, I'm one guy you can't blame for anything
